options.how: 1 to 4 players drop into a cave together; four classes (Scout, Gunner, Engineer, Driller) each cover a job the team needs to finish the mission.
Two teams of five fight over lanes; you can deny allied creeps below 50% health so the enemy loses the gold and experience.
Two teams of five; last hits on minions earn gold, but you cannot kill your own minions, so lane pressure comes only from attacking.

sources.note: Deep Rock Galactic: 1 to 4 player co-op FPS with four classes
Dota 2: allied units deniable below a health threshold, creeps at 50%
League of Legends: farming by last hitting minions; no deny mechanic

options.how: Four survivors must revive and cover each other against AI-spawned hordes; bots fill empty slots and players can join mid-campaign.
Deathmatch scores kills and subtracts suicides; Capture the Flag pits two teams stealing each other's flag.

sources.note: Left 4 Dead: four survivors, bots fill slots, players join at any time
Unreal Tournament: Deathmatch and Capture the Flag modes

options.how: Up to four chefs share one kitchen and one order queue, locally or online; the score belongs to the whole team.
Up to four players knock each other off the stage; damage percent raises launch distance and the last stock standing wins.

sources.note: Overcooked! 2: online and local co-op for up to four
Super Smash Bros. Melee: four-player Stock and Time battles

options.how: Up to 8 players per Battle.net game; a party shares experience, gold, quest progress and map locations.
Players race to destroy each other's bases on Battle.net, in unranked melee or ranked ladder games.

sources.note: Diablo II: parties share experience, gold, location and quest info
StarCraft: Battle.net melee and ladder play

options.how: The defuser sees the bomb but not the manual; experts hold the manual but cannot see the bomb. Only talking defuses it.
One-versus-one card duels; Ranked pairs you with opponents by rank and matchmaking rating.

sources.note: Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes: defuser and experts split information
Hearthstone: one-on-one matchmaking by MMR

options.how: The band earns one shared score; a failed player can be saved by a bandmate's Overdrive, and if the band meter empties everyone fails.
Versus mode puts two players side by side on one cabinet, each on their own pad, competing for the better score.

sources.note: Rock Band: shared band score and saving failed bandmates with Overdrive
Dance Dance Revolution: two-player Versus mode

options.how: Exactly two players, co-op only; the Friend's Pass lets one owner invite a second player free, so every level is built for a pair.
Up to 100 players parachute onto one map; a shrinking Blue Zone forces the crowd together until one player or squad is left.

sources.note: It Takes Two: Friend's Pass, one owner plus one guest
PUBG: Battlegrounds: up to 100 players, shrinking Blue Zone

options.game: Street Fighter II: The World Warrior
options.how: Strictly one on one; a second player can interrupt a CPU run with Here Comes a New Challenger and the winner keeps playing.
99 players play Tetris at once; line clears send garbage to a target you pick or let the game choose, and knockouts boost attacks.

sources.note: Street Fighter II: one-on-one versus, challenger interrupts
Tetris 99: 99-player battle royale with targeted garbage

options.how: A separate co-op campaign for two robots, Atlas and P-Body, each with a portal gun; chambers need four portals to solve.
Thousands of players fight across persistent continents; a record battle logged 1,158 players in one fight.

sources.note: Portal 2: two-player co-op campaign with Atlas and P-Body
PlanetSide 2: battles of thousands of players

options.how: One versus one over three locations and six simultaneous turns; either player can Snap to double the cube stakes.
Up to 150 players per match; your first death sends you to the Gulag for a 1v1 duel to earn a redeploy.

sources.note: Marvel Snap: 1v1, three locations, six turns, Snap doubles cubes
Call of Duty: Warzone: Gulag 1v1 redeploy

options.how: Two Yarnys tied by one thread; puzzles need one to anchor or pulley while the other climbs. Local co-op only.
Thousands of players split into two factions on one war map; each shard holds up to 4,000 and logistics are all player-run.

sources.note: Unravel Two: two tethered Yarnys, thread bridges and pulleys
Foxhole: persistent war between Colonials and Wardens

options.how: One persistent universe on a single shard (Tranquility); every player shares the same economy, space and history.
Short matches with a five-minute clock; ranked playlists of up to 3v3 reset the field every match.

sources.note: EVE Online: Tranquility single-shard cluster
Rocket League: ranked matchmaking and playlists

options.how: Each shard is a persistent world where player houses stay put, so one server's landscape differs from another's.
A match ends at the frag limit or time limit, then the next map starts clean with everyone at zero.

sources.note: Ultima Online: persistent online world with player housing
Quake III Arena: frag and time limits end a match

options.how: One shared world per region; zone colors set PvP risk, and territory, markets and gear persist between sessions.
Brief 1v1 battles matched by trophy count; each one ends and only trophies and rewards carry forward.

sources.note: Albion Online: one-world sandbox MMO with zone-based PvP
Clash Royale: matches by similar trophy count

options.how: Community-built persistent worlds run around the clock on player servers, with human DMs steering NPCs live.
Playlists drop parties into one-off matches; when the game ends the party returns to the lobby for the next.

sources.note: Neverwinter Nights: persistent worlds and community modules
Halo 2: matchmaking playlists and parties

options.how: Your character, skills and bank persist in a shared world; the Wilderness is a standing PvP zone you can walk into.
Online races of up to 12 players; each Grand Prix or race ends and a new lobby forms.

sources.note: RuneScape: persistent characters and Wilderness PvP
Mario Kart 8 Deluxe: online races of up to 12 players

options.how: The host screen shows a room code; friends join from any phone browser at jackbox.tv. No matchmaking with strangers.
Ladder matchmaking by MMR places players in leagues from Bronze to Grandmaster.

sources.note: The Jackbox Party Pack: join with a room code at jackbox.tv
StarCraft II: ladder leagues Bronze to Grandmaster

options.how: Deathmatch over IPX for up to four or by modem or serial cable for two: you set it up with the people you knew.
Xbox Live playlists matched parties automatically and gave each player a 1 to 50 skill level per ranked playlist.

sources.note: Doom: IPX four-player and serial or modem two-player games
Halo 2: 1 to 50 skill level per ranked playlist

options.how: No matchmaking: one player hosts and invites a crew of up to four through Steam friends before landing.
Ranked uses per-character League Points to pair similar players; at Master rank, Master Rate decides matches and standing.

sources.note: Lethal Company: host-and-invite co-op for up to four
Street Fighter 6: League Points and Master Rate ranked play

options.how: The host makes a private lobby for 4 to 15 and shares a code; social deduction works best among people who know each other.
You are matched against opponents with a similar trophy count; card levels are ignored by matchmaking.

sources.note: Among Us: private lobby with a code, 4 to 15 players
Clash Royale: matchmaking by trophy count

options.how: On Battle.net you create a named game, optionally with a password, and friends join it by name from the game list.
Ranked Solo/Duo uses placements and LP to move you through tiers; duo queuing is limited at the top tiers.

sources.note: Diablo II: Battle.net game creation with name and password
League of Legends: ranked tiers, divisions and queues

options.how: Co-op is hosted by one player who invites a partner; the host plays Atlas, the guest P-Body, and the host's progress drives the hub.
Battle.net offered ranked ladder games next to unranked melee, so players could see how they stacked up.

sources.note: Portal 2: host plays Atlas, guest plays P-Body
StarCraft: Battle.net ladder ranking

options.how: Every match starts with the same basic kit and loot found on the map; nothing you pick up carries to the next match.
Die in a raid and you lose everything you brought except melee, armband and secure container; insurance may return items.
Past early Bloodline ranks a hired hunter who dies is gone for good with their gear; only Bloodline progress is safe.

sources.note: Apex Legends: fixed starting kit, random loot each match
Escape from Tarkov: items lost on death except secure container
Hunt: Showdown: hunter and equipment lost on death

options.how: In red and black zones a killed player drops all equipped and carried gear for others to loot; yellow zones only knock down.
Dying adds a stacking health and energy penalty up to 60% that clears in town; no items or experience are lost.

sources.note: Albion Online: full-loot red and black zones
Guild Wars: death penalty capped at 60%, no item loss

options.how: Your corpse drops a backpack holding everything you carried; anyone can take it before it despawns.
Dead players respawn in timed waves at their spawn room with their loadout; nothing is dropped or lost.

sources.note: Rust: corpses drop a backpack with all their items
Team Fortress 2: wave respawn system

options.how: Die in the Wilderness and you keep only your most valuable items; a skulled player drops everything unprotected.
There is no inventory at stake in a match: you only win or lose the game and your rank.

sources.note: RuneScape: items kept on death and skull rules
Rocket League: rank and matchmaking per playlist

options.how: Gear taken into a dungeon is lost on death unless you reach an escape portal; other players can loot your body.
Fainting carts you back to camp; three faints fail the quest, but no gear or items are taken from you.

sources.note: Dark and Darker: extraction dungeon crawler
Monster Hunter: World: co-op hunts

options.how: Other players' messages, bloodstains replaying their deaths, and passing phantoms appear in your world without a live session.
All interaction is live: four players in one session, with bots filling empty slots. Nothing persists between groups.

sources.note: Dark Souls: messages, bloodstains and phantoms
Left 4 Dead: live four-player sessions with bots

options.how: Roads, bridges, signs and cargo other players built appear in your world once an area joins the network; you never meet them.
Another online player may join you live as a fellow traveler; nothing they do persists after they leave.

sources.note: Death Stranding: other players' structures appear in your world
Journey: play in the company of a fellow traveler online

options.how: Players upload courses to Course World; others play, like and leave comments on them long after they were made.
Every attack is live: garbage goes to opponents in the same 99-player match, and nothing carries outside it.

sources.note: Super Mario Maker 2: Course World uploads and feedback
Tetris 99: live 99-player matches

options.how: You raid other players' villages while they are offline; their base layout and defenses fight back on their behalf.
Both players are online and take turns live; there is no way to affect an opponent outside the match.

sources.note: Clash of Clans: build a village and army, attack opponents
Hearthstone: live one-on-one matches

options.how: One player is the Killer hunting the others; four Survivors try to escape before being hooked and sacrificed. Each side has its own rules.
Two teams of five; after 12 rounds the sides swap, so both teams play attack and defense on the same map.

sources.note: Dead by Daylight: 4 vs 1, one killer and four survivors
Counter-Strike 2: teams switch sides after the first half

options.how: Luigi's Ghost Mansion: the GamePad player is an invisible ghost; up to four flashlight holders hunt it and revive fainted friends.
Everyone spawns with the same tools and fights for the same map pickups; only aim and movement separate players.

sources.note: Nintendo Land: invisible ghost versus flashlight trackers
Quake III Arena: deathmatch with shared weapon pickups

options.how: Crewmates do tasks and vote; hidden Impostors kill, sabotage, fake tasks and travel through vents.
Teams of up to three drive cars with the same boost, jump and flip; only the goal you defend differs.

sources.note: Among Us: Crewmate and Impostor roles
Rocket League: 3v3 maximum in ranked

options.game: Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Pandora Tomorrow
options.how: Spies play in third person with stealth gadgets; mercenaries play in first person with guns and flashlights.
50 vs 50 where both armies pick from the same 14 roles across command, infantry, recon and armour.

sources.note: Splinter Cell: Pandora Tomorrow: Spies versus Mercenaries
Hell Let Loose: 50 vs 50, 14 roles

options.how: One button marks where you aim; context turns it into enemy, item or location callouts with voice lines, so no mic is needed.
Speech recognition lets the ghost, Spirit Box and Ouija Board hear what you say aloud; talking is play and a risk.

sources.note: Apex Legends: contextual ping system
Phasmophobia: voice recognition for ghost interaction

options.how: Proximity voice only carries nearby; walkie-talkies reach the rest of the crew, so who can hear you matters.
The laser pointer marks enemies, ore and objects so every teammate sees the marker through walls.

sources.note: Lethal Company: proximity voice and walkie-talkies
Deep Rock Galactic: marked targets visible through walls

options.how: Two players are split up in a castle; only walkie-talkie voice lets one describe what the other needs to solve.
No text or voice chat: companions can only chirp a musical call, which also recharges each other's scarves.

sources.note: We Were Here: separated players communicate by walkie-talkie
Journey: wordless online companion

options.how: Proximity, unit and command VoIP channels link squads, officers and the commander; the game says communication is essential.
Pinging marks enemies and interactables for the squad and posts an item's name and cost to chat, so runs coordinate without voice.

sources.note: Hell Let Loose: in-game proximity, command and unit VoIP; communication is essential
Risk of Rain 2: cost of purchasables added to their chat message when pinged; enemies and interactables can be pinged

options.how: The whole game is spoken description: the defuser explains the bomb aloud, experts read the manual and answer.
A laser pointer marks enemies and resources that every teammate sees through walls, so warnings land without anyone speaking.

sources.note: Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes: the defuser sees the bomb, experts have the manual, so players must talk
Deep Rock Galactic: marked enemies and objects can be seen through walls by all players

options.how: A player hosts the world from the game or runs the free dedicated server; up to 10 Vikings share a world file the host owns.
Bungie runs mission and physics hosts in its data centers and matchmakes players into shared spaces (hybrid with peer links).

sources.note: Valheim: local hosting or dedicated server, 10-player cap
Destiny 2: mission and physics hosts in Bungie data centers

options.how: Players run their own servers with modules built in the Aurora toolset, from four-friend campaigns to free persistent worlds.
The developer runs every shard; players pick a server and the world lives there whether they log in or not.

sources.note: Neverwinter Nights: community servers and persistent worlds
Ultima Online: Origin-run online world

options.how: Peer-to-peer: the players' own PCs run the game in lockstep over IPX or a modem, with no server at all.
The developer's servers hold each continent's war for thousands of players at once; nobody can host it themselves.

sources.note: Doom: peer-to-peer IPX and serial networking
PlanetSide 2: massive battles on developer-run servers

options.how: Host and Play runs the world on your own device and ends when you leave; or run TerrariaServer.exe so it stays up.
The developer runs the war shards, up to 4,000 players each; the war continues whether you are logged in or not.

sources.note: Terraria: Host and Play or dedicated server software
Foxhole: persistent war on developer shards

options.how: Communities rent or run their own servers with custom maps, rules and admins; players browse and join them.
Ubisoft hosts every ranked and casual match on its own servers; players cannot run official servers.

sources.note: Counter-Strike 1.6: community-run servers
Rainbow Six Siege: Ubisoft-hosted matches

options.how: Roads and structures other players built appear in your world once areas connect; you like their bridges and donate to shared projects.
Built purely for two players in live couch or online co-op; partners only affect each other while playing together.

sources.note: Death Stranding 2: Social Strand System for asynchronous connection; other players' roads and structures become usable
It Takes Two: built purely for two, couch or online co-op

options.how: Victims rely on stealth to find tools and escape, while Family players track them down and stop them; each side has different goals.
Each player controls one footballer in teams of 3, 4 or 5; both sides have identical abilities, so skill and teamwork decide matches.

sources.note: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre: victims use stealth to escape, Family players track them down
Rematch: control one player in online football, teams of 3, 4 or 5
